new_statements.rule_in_words: According to the StressTyp classification (second-hand, from Breen's unpublished AIATSIS manuscript), Bularnu has main stress on the first syllable of the word with secondary stress on alternate syllables thereafter; the quantity-sensitive flag says syllable weight plays a marginal role (the language is otherwise quantity-insensitive), but the appendix does not say what that marginal weight effect is.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on alternate syllables after the initial main stress (category I heading); whether a final syllable may carry secondary stress is not indicated.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the 'quantity-sensitive' flag: marginal quantity-sensitivity. No E (many exceptions) or M (morphology) code is attached to Bularnu.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (appendix classifies word-stress type); the primary description is Breen's unpublished manuscript, which was not opened, so nothing about citation forms vs phrases can be checked.
new_statements.identity_note: Bularnu = AIATSIS G12.1, Tindale T246, no ISO code (Ethnologue folded it into Yindjilandji [yil]); Breen's main informants (Didgeroo Jack, Ivy Monkhouse) may actually have spoken the Dhidhani/Dhidhanu dialect (G42), per Breen 1971 entry 50; Breen 1988:1 treats Dhidhanu, Baringkirri (G51) and Indjiladji (G52) as dialects of Bularnu. The Goedemans entry refers to Bularnu as a whole (Breen's ms). Do not confuse with 'Bularnu' as a Tindale synonym of Yaroinga/Andegerebinha (G12), which is Arandic.

tone.quote: Breen (1974:5) notes that phonetically “the stressed (i.e. first) vowel in a disyllabic word is long if the following consonant is a voiced stop ... and is short if the following consonant is voiceless”. The words with VVt (plus one with VVp) are exceptions to this phonetic generalisation so it appears that vowel length is contrastive in Bularnu, in which case there is no phonemic voicing contrast for the apico-alveolar stop position
